headline: Proves a pushed fluid can run any program: a marked particle enters a fixed box exactly when the program halts.
scope: Smooth forced incompressible Navier–Stokes flows in three dimensions, starting from rest at any fixed positive computable viscosity. Nine companion papers vary the domain and force conditions.
plain: A Turing machine is a simple model of any computer program. These nine papers turn any such machine and its input into a recipe for pushing a thick fluid, like honey in a box. The fluid starts at rest. One marked drop of fluid reaches a fixed target region exactly when the program stops. Since no method can decide in general whether a program stops, no method can decide in general where that drop goes.
doesNot: This does not say that natural, unforced fluid flows compute, and it says nothing about whether Navier–Stokes solutions can blow up. The force is designed by hand for each program and input.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: It moves fluid computation from specially chosen geometries to a fixed flat domain, with viscosity and a fluid at rest. Lean covers several versions.

explanation:
Start with a simple flow on a cube whose opposite faces are glued, called a flat torus. Let the fluid move only in the X direction, with speed A(t)·sin(2πY). Here Y is height and A(t) is a strength you choose. This flow is incompressible: it never squeezes the fluid. For this flow the fluid needs no pressure. The force only has to speed it up and beat friction. With viscosity ν = 1 and A(t) = t, the needed force is (1 + 4π²t)·sin(2πY). At height Y = 1/4 and time 1 this is about 40.48. A drop at that height travels t²/2, so 0.5 units by time 1.

This is the basic trick. The Navier–Stokes equations describe a viscous, incompressible fluid. Viscosity is its internal friction. If you choose the motion first, the force that produces it is just acceleration minus the friction term[7]. So the hard part is not the force. It is to choose a motion that runs a program, written from the program's table of rules without running it first[8].

A Turing machine is a simple model of a computer: a tape of symbols, a head, and a finite table of rules. It halts if it reaches a stop state. One step of the machine can erase information, but a smooth flow can always be run backward[3]. So the papers keep a record of past steps, an idea going back to Bennett[4]. Each step then becomes a reversible map on small rectangles or boxes. Shear flows like the one above carry out these maps[13].

Earlier fluid computers used steady flows on specially shaped spaces. Cardona, Miranda, Peralta-Salas and Presas built one on a reshaped three-sphere[5]. Here the space is flat and fixed, and the fluid starts at rest[6].

Take any machine and input. The papers claim a smooth force where a fixed particle enters a fixed region exactly when the machine halts[1]. So deciding where the particle goes is undecidable: no general method can answer it[2]. Variants make the force constant after time one[9], or let force and velocity fade faster than any power of time[10]. In another, the velocity at a fixed spot reveals halting[11]. The last paper puts the whole flow in one bounded region of ordinary space[12].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal statements of several versions. They include the sheet maps, the fading-force memory, the velocity tests and the bounded-region computer in ordinary space. So those are proved, as far as the Lean statements match the papers. Other variants, such as the eventually constant force, are claims only. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: Lean statements cover several of the main constructions. The forces are hand-built for each program; this says nothing about natural flows or about Navier–Stokes blowup. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: The equations of motion for a viscous fluid, like water or honey.
The fluid is never squeezed or stretched in volume; its velocity has zero divergence.
The internal friction of a fluid, written ν.
A cube whose opposite faces are glued, so fluid leaving one side comes back on the other.
A simple model of a computer: a tape of symbols, a moving head, and a finite table of rules.
A Turing machine reaching its stop state after finitely many steps.
No single method can give the right yes-or-no answer for every case.
A flow where layers slide past each other at different speeds.
